result: Curvature domains exist in V4 as sub-millimeter sized modules (mean = 434 μm) that are spatially distinct from color, high spatial frequency, and straight orientation domains, and are located largely within the orientation bands of V4.
evaluation: Claims C14-C32 provide converging evidence from optical imaging data across three cases showing curvature domains exist, have appropriate size (C31), are spatially distinct from other functional domains (C22-C23, C26-C27), and fall within orientation bands (C25, C28). The quantitative overlap analyses and domain size measurements support these conclusions.

result: Curvature domains exhibit strong selectivity for curved stimuli over straight stimuli, while color, high spatial frequency, and straight orientation domains show minimal response to curvature stimuli. This selectivity is maintained across both curved gratings and curved lines.
evaluation: Claims C33-C43 demonstrate functional selectivity through timecourse analyses and statistical comparisons (Wilcoxon tests) showing curvature domains respond preferentially to curved stimuli while other domain types do not (C34, C36, C37). The consistency across stimulus types (gratings and lines, C40, C43) strengthens the conclusion.

result: Curvature preferring domains were not observed in V1, consistent with previous literature.
evaluation: Claims C44 and C110 report negative findings in V1 supported by experimental data (Figure 2—figure supplement 10) and consistent with multiple cited studies (Yue et al., 2014; Ponce et al., 2017). This supports V4 as the curvature-emergent area.

result: Correlation analysis of curvature maps reveals a systematic organization where higher correlation values occur between maps of similar curvature degree, with declining correlation as curvature difference increases, suggesting a shifting map of curvature degree.
evaluation: Claims C45-C50 describe correlation analyses (Figure 3B-C) showing systematic relationships between map similarity and curvature degree difference. The declining correlation with increasing curvature difference (C49-C50) supports the inference of systematic organization, though the relationship is not necessarily linear.

result: High correlation values occur only between curvature gratings of the same orientation, while low correlation values occur between different curvature orientations and between curved and straight gratings.
evaluation: Claims C51-C53 describe correlation analyses for curvature orientation (Figure 4C) showing orientation-specific organization. The pattern of high correlation for matched orientations and low correlation for mismatched orientations supports systematic curvature orientation mapping.

result: Curvature domains contain subregions with high curvature preference that exhibit graded responses to curvature degree, with response magnitudes gradually diminishing with curvature degree difference.
evaluation: Claims C54-C56 describe subdomain organization within curvature domains (Figure 5) showing preference for high over low curvature and graded responses. The experimental data support hierarchical organization within curvature domains.

result: Paired opposing curvature orientations occupy roughly complementary positions within curvature domains, with preferences maintained across curved gratings and lines. On average, 22.4% of pixels within curvature domains respond to two opposite orientations.
evaluation: Claims C57-C60 describe curvature orientation organization (Figure 6) showing complementary spatial arrangement of opposing orientations with quantified overlap (C60). The consistency across stimulus types (C58-C59) and quantitative overlap analysis support the conclusion of complementary organization.

result: Spatial progressions from straight to curved domains exist in V4, with curvature preference generally progressing from low to high curvature with distance across cortex. However, diversity in organization exists, including domains with broad curvature preference, indicating complex curvature representation.
evaluation: Claims C61-C66 describe spatial progressions (Figure 7) showing systematic organization from straight to curved domains. The quantitative distance analysis (C63-C64) supports the general trend, while acknowledging variability (C65-C66). The complexity is appropriately characterized rather than oversimplified.

result: Curvature domains do not co-localize with orientation pinwheel centers, and curvature responses are not simply a weighted sum of responses to component orientations.
evaluation: Claims C67-C71 address alternative explanations through spatial analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 12) and response magnitude comparisons (Figure 7—figure supplement 2). The statistical test (p=0.13, C69) and order-of-magnitude difference in component responses (C71) support rejection of these alternative explanations.

result: While end-stopping may contribute to curvature computation, curvature domains are not simply end-stopped domains. End-stopping and curvature maps are spatially distinct (66.7% non-overlapping), and curvature domains show stronger responses to curved than to small straight stimuli.
evaluation: Claims C72-C80, C99-C104 address the relationship between end-stopping and curvature through spatial overlap analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 13) showing 66.7% spatial distinctness (C78) and differential response patterns (C79). The integration of literature (C72-C75, C99-C102) with experimental data supports the conclusion that end-stopping contributes but is not sufficient.

result: There is a systematic map of curvature representation in V4 that is distinct from maps for straight orientation, color, high spatial frequency, orientation pinwheels, and end-stopping. Curvature domains exhibit selectivity for degree of curvature mapping in a spatially shifting manner, with multiple types of organizations including sequences of curvature degree and domains with complex curvature preference.
evaluation: Claims C81-C88 summarize the major findings integrating evidence from multiple experiments. The systematic mapping (C81-C82), distinctness from other maps (C83), and organizational complexity (C84-C85, C88) are supported by the collective experimental evidence. The non-linear progressions (C85) and stimulus consistency (C86) are appropriately characterized.

result: The authors propose a model where straight and curved regions co-exist and occupy roughly complementary territory within the orientation bands of V4, suggesting a possible 'curvature hypercolumn' within V4.
evaluation: Claims C87, C18, and C89 propose a hypercolumn model based on the experimental findings. While the data support spatial organization and complementarity, the hypercolumn concept is explicitly proposed as a model requiring further testing. The novelty claim (C89) is a statement about literature rather than experimental validation.

result: Curvature domain responses result from a non-linear integration of straight oriented inputs rather than a simple linear combination of local orientation domain responses.
evaluation: Claims C90-C91 propose a mechanistic interpretation based on the spatial distinctness and weak component responses. While the data rule out simple linear summation, the positive claim of 'non-linear (perhaps multi-step) integration' is speculative and not directly tested. The inference is reasonable but requires additional experiments for validation.

result: Curvature domains differ from high spatial frequency maps (less than 15% overlap) and have little overlap with low spatial frequency domains. Similar curvature maps were obtained with different curvature degrees and with gratings versus lines, while scrambled stimuli failed to produce curvature maps.
evaluation: Claims C92-C98 address whether curvature responses are due to spatial frequency content through multiple control experiments. The low overlap with high SF domains (C93), similarity across curvature degrees (C94) and stimulus types (C95), failure of scrambled stimuli (C96), and low overlap with low SF domains (C97) collectively support that curvature representation is distinct from spatial frequency.

result: The findings are consistent with a hierarchical view where V1 is the 'orientation-emergent' area, V2 is the 'cue-invariant orientation-emergent' area, and V4 is the 'curvature-emergent' area. The curvature domains identified here correspond to the posterior curvature-biased patch (PCP) described by Yue et al. (2014), and may contribute to higher-level object, face, and body representations.
evaluation: Claims C105-C115 integrate current findings with prior literature to propose a hierarchical framework. The correspondence with Yue et al.'s PCP patch (C108-C109) is supported by anatomical location and scale. The hierarchical characterization (C111-C113) is well-established in the field. The predictions about higher-level contributions (C114-C115) are appropriately framed as speculative.

result: Methodological details: experiments were conducted in accordance with NIH guidelines and institutional approval, imaging V4 at 0-5° eccentricity, using curvature stimuli designed based on ellipse formula with different a/b ratios, with 4° stimulus size matching V4 receptive field sizes.
evaluation: Claims C116-C120 describe methodological details that are standard reporting requirements. The ethical compliance (C116), anatomical targeting (C117), stimulus design (C118-C119), and size justification (C120 with citation) are appropriately documented.

result: Background and hypothesis: V1 and V2 contain orientation domains, V4 neurons respond to curvature, but curvature maps had not been demonstrated. The authors hypothesized that orientation bands in V4 include both orientation and curvature domains, and that key emergent functions at each cortical stage are represented in systematic, modular maps.
evaluation: Claims C1-C13, C19 establish the background and hypothesis. The prior work on V1/V2 orientation domains (C1-C4) and V4 curvature responses (C5-C6) is well-cited. The knowledge gaps (C7, C12) and hypothesis (C13) appropriately frame the study. The broader framework (C19) is an inference combining current and prior work.
